client: I started this new job in marketing about six weeks ago, and honestly, it's been really hard. Everyone around me seems so confident and experienced, and I just feel like I'm constantly falling behind — like no matter how much I work, I can't keep up with the deadlines. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is just... real, and I don't see how sitting here fixes that.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed — starting a new job is genuinely demanding, and the pressure you're describing is real, not something you're imagining or exaggerating. I also hear your skepticism about whether talking helps, and I think that's actually a really honest and important thing to name right at the start. What I'm curious about is this: when you say everyone around you seems more confident and experienced, what specific moments or interactions are making you feel that way?

client: Honestly, it's little things that pile up throughout the day. Like yesterday in a team meeting, someone asked a question about a process and everyone else just nodded along like they totally got it, and I had no idea what they were talking about but I just smiled and pretended I did. And then afterward my manager made this offhand comment about how the team "hits the ground running," and I just felt this sinking feeling like... I'm the only one who's still stumbling.
therapist: That moment sounds really uncomfortable — sitting in that meeting, feeling like everyone else had a map you weren't given, and then your manager's comment landing like a confirmation of your worst fear. I want to gently point something out though: you interpreted everyone's nodding as *understanding*, but is it possible some of them were doing exactly what you were — keeping up appearances in a room where nobody wants to look lost? What do you think it would take for you to feel like it was safe enough to ask a question out loud in one of those meetings?

client: I mean, maybe you're right that some of them were faking it too, but it doesn't really feel that way in the moment — it feels like I'm the only one drowning. And as for asking a question out loud... honestly, the thought of that makes my stomach drop, because what if I ask something that confirms everyone's suspicions that I don't belong there? My manager's comment is still ringing in my ears, and it's hard to imagine taking that kind of risk when I already feel like I'm on thin ice.
therapist: That fear — that one question could confirm you don't belong — is such a common and painful thought, but I want to gently examine it with you: right now it feels like certainty, but what's the actual evidence that your colleagues *already* suspect you don't belong, versus this being something your anxious mind is predicting? It's also worth noticing that you've been holding this together for six weeks, navigating unfamiliar territory while managing everyone's perceptions — that takes a lot of energy, and it's not nothing. What do you think it says about you that you're still showing up every day, even while feeling this way?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically there's probably no hard proof that they suspect anything... but it doesn't really feel that way when I'm in the room with them. Like, there was this moment last week where my manager asked me to clarify something in a meeting, and even though it was probably a normal question, my whole body just went into panic mode, convinced that was the moment everything would unravel. And as for showing up every day... I guess I do that, but honestly it feels less like strength and more like I just don't have a choice.
therapist: That gap you're describing — knowing something logically but your body reacting as if danger is real — is actually at the heart of what makes anxiety so exhausting, because your nervous system doesn't wait for evidence before sounding the alarm. And I want to sit with what you said about showing up feeling like "no choice" rather than strength, because I wonder if part of you has learned to dismiss your own resilience so automatically that it doesn't even register as something you're doing. When you imagine a version of yourself who *did* see that daily showing-up as meaningful — even just a little — what would feel different about how you walked into that office?

client: I guess... if I actually believed showing up meant something, maybe I wouldn't feel so invisible when I walk in there. Like maybe I'd hold my head up a little instead of just trying to blend into the walls and get through the day without anyone noticing how much I'm struggling. But honestly, that feels almost impossible to imagine right now, because the moment I walk through that door, the anxiety just takes over and any sense of "I did something hard" completely disappears.
therapist: That image you just painted — of holding your head up instead of trying to disappear into the walls — feels really significant, because you could actually picture it, even if only for a moment, which means some part of you knows that version of yourself exists. What you're describing sounds like anxiety is essentially ambushing you at the door, wiping out any sense of your own capability before you even get a chance to use it. I'm wondering if we could think about something very small — not a leap of confidence, just a tiny experiment — like one thing you could do *before* you walk through that door that might help you carry even a small reminder of your own strength into the room with you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I like that you called it a "tiny experiment" because the word "experiment" makes it feel less like I have to get it right. But honestly, I'm already trying to think of what that one thing could be, and my mind just goes blank — like even the idea of preparing something feels like another thing I could fail at. I guess I'm worried that whatever I come up with, anxiety will just bulldoze right through it anyway.
therapist: The fact that your mind immediately turned toward "what if I fail at this too" is actually really useful information — it shows how quickly that self-critical voice moves in to shut things down before you've even begun, and that pattern is worth noticing in itself. I want to reassure you that there's no wrong answer here, and honestly, even *noticing* that anxiety bulldozed through something is valuable data, not failure — that's what makes it an experiment rather than a test. So with that pressure off, I'm curious: is there anything, even something that seems almost too small or silly to mention, that has ever given you even a brief moment of steadiness before a stressful situation?

client: I appreciate you framing it as an experiment, but honestly, my brain doesn't really buy that in the moment — it still feels like a test no matter what I tell myself. But... I guess there is one thing. Sometimes when I'm really dreading something, like before a work presentation, I'll go to the bathroom and just run cold water over my wrists for a minute, and it does something — like it kind of interrupts the spiral for a second. I've never told anyone that because it sounds so weird and small.
therapist: That doesn't sound weird at all — it actually sounds like you've intuitively discovered something really grounded in how our nervous system works, where a physical sensation can interrupt the anxiety spiral in a way that words sometimes can't. The fact that you found that on your own, without anyone teaching you, tells me you have more capacity for self-soothing than you're giving yourself credit for. I'm wondering — what would it feel like to deliberately use that tomorrow morning, not as a fix, but just as a small act of showing up for yourself before the day takes over?

client: I mean... it's kind of nice to hear that it's not just some weird thing I do, but I'm not sure I'd call it a "capacity for self-soothing" — it feels more like I just stumbled onto something by accident. And the idea of doing it deliberately tomorrow morning feels a little forced, like if I plan it out it'll lose whatever made it work in the first place. I guess I'm worried I'll do it and still feel just as anxious, and then I'll have failed at the one thing that was actually helping me.
therapist: That worry makes a lot of sense — there's something fragile about a coping tool that feels accidental, like naming it too loudly might break the spell. But I want to gently turn that fear around: if you do it deliberately tomorrow and still feel anxious, that wouldn't mean it failed, it would just mean anxiety showed up anyway *and* you did something kind for yourself in the middle of it — which is actually a different kind of success than "feeling better." What if the goal tomorrow wasn't to feel less anxious, but just to notice whether that moment at the sink feels like anything at all — even one percent of steadiness?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I like the idea of reframing it as "noticing" rather than "fixing" — that feels a little less pressure. But honestly, I'm worried that if I go to the sink tomorrow with this whole intention behind it, it'll feel forced and self-conscious, like I'm performing a ritual instead of just... existing for a second. What if that self-awareness is exactly what kills the tiny bit of calm I accidentally found there?
therapist: That's such a perceptive thing to notice — that self-consciousness itself can become another layer of pressure, turning a quiet moment into something you're watching yourself perform. Here's what strikes me though: you're already being deeply self-aware right now, in this conversation, and yet something real is still happening here — you're reflecting, connecting, finding words for things you've never said out loud before. What if that same self-awareness that feels like a threat could sometimes be the thing that actually keeps you company, rather than judges you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it feels like a stretch. Like, right now it feels okay because you're here responding to me, so there's a reason for the self-awareness — it's serving a purpose. But when I'm alone, that same watching-myself feeling just turns into this cold, critical voice that points out everything I'm doing wrong, even something as simple as sitting on the couch. I don't know how to make it feel like company instead of a judge.
therapist: What you just described — that inner voice that follows you even to the couch and finds fault there — sounds genuinely exhausting, like you can never fully rest because the critic is always on duty. It's really meaningful that you can already see the difference between self-awareness that feels connected and purposeful versus the cold, judging kind, because that distinction is actually the beginning of being able to relate to that voice differently rather than just being ruled by it. I'm curious — if you had to describe that critical voice, does it remind you of anyone, or does it have a particular tone to it, like someone you've heard before?
